title: Debugging Containers
subtitle: Logs, exec, inspect, stats — the complete toolkit for diagnosing containerised applications

content.code:
# View all logs since container started
docker logs my-api

# Follow (stream) logs in real time
docker logs -f my-api

# Show only last 50 lines
docker logs --tail 50 my-api

# Show logs with timestamps
docker logs -t my-api

# Show logs since a specific time
docker logs --since 1h my-api       # last hour
docker logs --since 2024-01-15 my-api

# Combine: tail + follow with timestamps
docker logs -f -t --tail 100 my-api

# With Docker Compose:
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose logs -f --tail 50 api postgres

content.text: exec — run commands inside a running container

content.code:
# Open an interactive shell (bash)
docker exec -it my-api bash

# Alpine-based images use sh not bash
docker exec -it my-api sh

# Run a single command and exit
docker exec my-api node --version
docker exec my-api cat /app/config.json
docker exec my-api env | sort          # see all environment variables

# Connect to PostgreSQL inside its container
docker exec -it my-postgres psql -U postgres myapp

# Connect to Redis CLI
docker exec -it my-redis redis-cli

# With Compose:
docker compose exec api sh
docker compose exec postgres psql -U postgres myapp

# Debugging: what processes are running inside?
docker exec my-api ps aux

# Check disk usage inside container
docker exec my-api df -h

# Full JSON dump of a container's config
docker inspect my-api

# Extract specific fields with --format (Go template)
docker inspect my-api --format '{{.State.Status}}'
docker inspect my-api --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'
docker inspect my-api --format '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}'
docker inspect my-api --format '{{json .HostConfig.PortBindings}}'

# Live resource usage for all containers
docker stats
# CONTAINER     CPU %   MEM USAGE / LIMIT   MEM %   NET I/O   BLOCK I/O
# my-api        2.3%    128MiB / 512MiB     25%     1.2MB/...  0B
# my-postgres   0.1%    67MiB / 1GiB        6.5%    ...

# One-shot snapshot (no live update)
docker stats --no-stream

# See ALL containers including stopped ones
docker ps -a
# STATUS: Exited (1) 2 minutes ago  ← non-zero exit = crash

# Read the crash logs
docker logs my-api
# Error: ECONNREFUSED — database not ready yet

# Check exit code
docker inspect my-api --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'
# 1 = general error, 137 = OOM killed, 143 = SIGTERM (clean stop)

# Common exit codes:
# 0 = clean exit
# 1 = application error
# 137 = OOM kill (increase --memory limit)
# 139 = segfault
# 143 = SIGTERM received

# Debug a container that exits immediately:
# Override the CMD to keep it open
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myapp
# Now you're inside — diagnose manually

content.text: Add a /health endpoint to every service. A simple GET /health route that returns 200 gives you a compose healthcheck target, lets load balancers route traffic away from unhealthy instances, and is the first thing to check when debugging: docker exec my-api curl -s localhost:3000/health

questions.question: A container keeps restarting. docker ps shows 'Restarting (137) X seconds ago'. What does exit code 137 mean and what should you check?
options: The application threw a JavaScript error — check the source code
The container was OOM-killed (Out Of Memory) — increase the --memory limit or find a memory leak
The container received SIGTERM — check your restart policy
A dependency service wasn't ready — add depends_on with healthcheck
questions.explanation: Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL signal number). This happens when the kernel's OOM killer terminates the container because it exceeded its memory limit. Check docker stats to see memory usage. Either increase the memory limit (--memory 1g) or profile the application for memory leaks.

faq.q: How do I debug a container that doesn't have bash or sh installed?
faq.a: Use 'docker run --pid=container:<id> --network=container:<id> --privileged nicolaka/netshoot' — a debug container that shares the target container's PID and network namespace, giving you curl, dig, tcpdump, and many other tools without modifying your production image. Or use 'docker debug' (Docker Desktop feature) which attaches a debug shell to any container.

examples: docker logs --since 5m my-api | grep ERROR — quickly find recent errors in production without SSH-ing to the server
docker stats --no-stream | sort -k4 -h — sort all containers by memory usage to find the memory hog
